claims.claim: ice is slippery because of a thin near-surface water layer, not because of standing water or pressure alone
claims.definition: the modern explanation of ice friction: a molecular-scale liquid-like layer at the ice-air interface, fed by premelting and by frictional heating during sliding, lubricates the contact
claims.measured_value: qualitative: slipperiness arises from the near-surface water film; no single-number claim
claims.authoritative_source: Rosenberg, 'Why is ice slippery?', Physics Today 58(12), 50 (2005); Dash, Fu & Wettlaufer, 'The premelting of ice and its environmental consequences', Reviews of Geophysics (1995)
claims.notes: narration stays qualitative; no numeric claims

nuance.note: overall slipperiness mechanism: premelting/molecular mobility emphasized by current research, with complex temperature/pressure/speed dependence and newer self-lubrication proposals (Rosenberg 2005; recent literature) — not a single settled mechanism

claims.claim: a skater's pressure lowers ice's melting point by only a fraction of a degree, far too little to create the water film
claims.definition: Clausius-Clapeyron: melting point drops roughly 0.007 degrees Celsius per atmosphere; typical skate pressures correspond to a few atmospheres, so the shift is fractions of a degree
claims.measured_value: melting-point depression of order hundredths to tenths of a degree Celsius under skate pressure; narration says 'a fraction of a degree'
claims.authoritative_source: Rosenberg, 'Why is ice slippery?', Physics Today 58(12), 50 (2005); standard Clausius-Clapeyron treatment of the ice-water boundary
claims.notes: narration deliberately avoids the per-atmosphere coefficient; 'fraction of a degree' is the defensible center

nuance.note: Clausius-Clapeyron melting-point depression magnitude is textbook physics

claims.claim: a quasi-liquid layer exists on the ice surface even below the melting point
claims.definition: surface premelting: the topmost molecular layers of ice lose their rigid order and become liquid-like at temperatures below 0 degrees Celsius; proposed by Faraday and confirmed by modern surface studies
claims.measured_value: nanometre-scale liquid-like layer detected on ice below freezing; thickness varies with temperature and technique
claims.authoritative_source: Dash, Fu & Wettlaufer, 'The premelting of ice and its environmental consequences', Reviews of Geophysics (1995); Somorjai & Li, 'Surface melting of ice', Progress in Surface Science (1997)
claims.notes: narration says 'thin skin of water' without pinning a thickness

nuance.note: surface premelting / quasi-liquid layer is well documented experimentally (Dash et al. 1995); its detailed structure remains studied

claims.claim: frictional heating during glide warms the contact and feeds the near-surface water film
claims.definition: sliding friction dissipates work as heat at the blade-ice interface; at typical glide speeds this warming supplies meltwater to the contact and is a major contributor to low friction
claims.measured_value: qualitative: friction heating contributes to the lubricating film during glide; narration avoids speed/temperature specifics
claims.authoritative_source: Rosenberg, 'Why is ice slippery?', Physics Today 58(12), 50 (2005); Lozowski, Szilder & Maw, 'A model of ice skate lubrication' (2013)
claims.notes: narration says friction feeds the film faster than it can refreeze; no numbers

nuance.note: frictional heating contribution to the water film is well established; its relative share vs premelting is quantitatively debated

claims.claim: the quasi-liquid film thins as temperature falls, so blade behavior changes between mild and deep cold
claims.definition: premelted layer thickness decreases with decreasing temperature; with less lubricating water, the blade's grip and glide characteristics change, which is why ice behaves differently at mild versus deep frost
claims.measured_value: qualitative: film thickness decreases as temperature drops; narration uses minus five and minus thirty as illustrative conditions without claiming measured thresholds
claims.authoritative_source: Dash, Fu & Wettlaufer, 'The premelting of ice and its environmental consequences', Reviews of Geophysics (1995); Rosenberg, Physics Today (2005)
claims.notes: narration spells out 'minus five' and 'minus thirty' as conditions only; no threshold claimed

nuance.note: film thickness/behavior vs temperature is qualitative and complex; precise dependence modeled, not settled
